newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-Lawmakers tap support for open power markets.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Lawmakers tap support for open power markets.

text.p: Despite endless hours of hearings in Washington, House lawmakers need to go around the country to drum up support for requiring states to break up utility monopolies, analysts said Friday.

At the second of four hearings designed to preach the benefits of customer choice around the country, lawmakers Friday heard the same mix of advocates and critics of federal legislation as they heard Monday in Atlanta.

Two more hearings will be held in early May in Dallas and Chicago. None were scheduled by Republican Reps. Thomas Bliley of Virginia and Dan Schaefer of Colorado in the West, where consumers who get cheap hydroelectric power fear that power supply competition could push their bills higher, not lower.
For those looking to keep monopolies intact, the field hearings are a great way to slow down federal legislation that would require states to open local markets to competition.

But consumers resisting an open market criticized the hearings. "These hearings today are just a cheerleading session for proposals benefiting large industrial consumers and power purchasers," Wenonah Hauter from consumer group Citizen Action said at the Richmond meeting.
Those pushing for federal action said the hearings were needed to convince consumers that competition among power suppliers will be good for them.
For politicians, the longer they debate deregulation of the $200 billion electric industry, the more cash they can haul in from lobbyists.
"I think they're trying to wring as much campaign contributions out of this as possible," said Irwin Stelzer, regulatory policy studies director at the American Enterprise Institute.
"They're not insensitive to the fact that they have an entire industry by its wires," he said.

Industry analysts said at least two of the hearing cities were picked with conservative House leaders in mind. Atlanta is House Speaker Newt Gingrich's territory, and Dallas is in House Republican leader Dick Armey and Republican Whip Tom DeLay's home state.
Those pushing competition have to convince conservatives that federal legislation forcing states to give up control over local electricity sales would not trample states' rights.
"Part of the traveling around is to ... enable (lawmakers) to say in the end, 'We've considered individual states and there is an overriding national purpose for this,'" said Stelzer.

Analysts said the hearings were useful to educate the public, especially those who believe that big industrial users would gain the most in an open power market, while smaller users would be left to shoulder the costs of utility assets.

"It's not that big dogs are going to be eating first. They're already eating," said Wayne Crews, a fellow at the Competitive Enterprise Institute, which is pushing more radical deregulation than Schaefer and Bliley are seeking.
